claim: Pupil dilation increased monotonically with the number of LC spikes.
source: The magnitude of pupil responses following a spike cluster (quantified in a 6-s window from cluster onset) progressively increased with cluster size (the number of spikes in a cluster, Figure 1c, d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing progressive increase in pupil responses with cluster size, as shown in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: A positive, monotonic relationship exists between peak pupil diameter and LC cluster size in the majority of paired recordings.
source: Overall, we found a positive, monotonic relationship between peak pupil diameter and LC cluster size in the majority of paired recordings (linear regression R2 > 0.6 in 13 out of 19 paired recordings, Figure 1e), in line with previous findings in nonhuman primates (Varazzani et al., 2015; Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis showing R2 > 0.6 in 13 out of 19 recordings, and corroborated by citations to previous work in nonhuman primates.

claim: The latency of peak pupil diameter did not systematically vary with cluster size and ranged between 2.5 and 4 s.
source: The latency of peak pupil diameter did not systematically vary with cluster size and ranged between 2.5 and 4 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing latency measurements.

claim: This latency is consistent with our previous report.
source: This latency is consistent with our previous report (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the same authors.

claim: Substantial variations existed in the pupil-LC relationship with linear slopes ranging from 0.12 to 0.51.
source: However, substantial variations existed in the relationship (linear slopes ranging from 0.12 to 0.51. 0.24 ± 0.11, mean ± standard deviation [SD], n = 13), indicating variable couplings between pupil and LC neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of linear slopes from 13 recordings.

claim: Only peak pupil diameter associated with large clusters (≥5–6 spikes) can achieve a performance threshold of d′ = 1.
source: However, only peak pupil diameter associated with large clusters (≥5–6 spikes) can achieve a performance threshold of d′ = 1 (translates to ~0.75 area under the curve Simpson and Fitter, 1973, Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 1g and citation to Simpson and Fitter, 1973 for the d′ threshold translation.

claim: Larger clusters occurred less frequently.
source: Since larger clusters occurred less frequently (Figure 1d, h, Figure 1—figure supplement 5), our data suggest that pupil dilation cannot accurately represent the majority of LC spiking activity but can serve as a good proxy for the infrequent (<10%) and strong LC activity in real time (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by occurrence data shown in Figure 1d, h, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Pupil dilation cannot accurately represent the majority of LC spiking activity but can serve as a good proxy for the infrequent (<10%) and strong LC activity in real time.
source: Since larger clusters occurred less frequently (Figure 1d, h, Figure 1—figure supplement 5), our data suggest that pupil dilation cannot accurately represent the majority of LC spiking activity but can serve as a good proxy for the infrequent (<10%) and strong LC activity in real time (Figure 1h).
evidence: Inferred from the combination of occurrence data and ROC analysis showing that only large, infrequent clusters can be accurately predicted.

claim: A wide range of spike counts preceded pupil events of similar sizes.
source: However, a wide range of spike counts preceded pupil events of similar sizes (Figure 2b, c).
evidence: Supported by probability distributions shown in Figure 2b and 2c.

claim: Only LC activity preceding the infrequent (<10%), large dilation events (>1.5–2 SD) performed beyond 75% threshold.
source: However, only LC activity preceding the infrequent (<10%), large dilation events (>1.5–2 SD, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) performed beyond 75% threshold (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 2e and occurrence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only large pupil events can achieve good predictions of LC activity.
source: Similar to the previous results (Figure 1g), we found that only large pupil events can achieve good predictions (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The infrequent (<10%) but strong (>1.5–2 SD) pupil dilation events can be used to accurately and reliably predict LC activity in real time.
source: Taken together, our data show that pupil diameter and LC spiking are well correlated in a graded manner and that the infrequent (<10%) but strong (>1.5–2 SD) pupil dilation events can be used to accurately and reliably predict LC activity in real time.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of Figures 1 and 2 showing that only large, infrequent events achieve good prediction performance.

claim: An excitable volume on the order of 0.05–0.1 mm3 contains hundreds of LC neurons.
source: Based on the stimulation parameters, we estimated an excitable volume on the order of 0.05–0.1 mm3, containing hundreds of LC neurons (Figure 3a, b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Methods).
evidence: Based on calculation using stimulation parameters and tissue properties as described in Methods.

claim: Waveforms from the putatively same units were more similar than the waveforms from the putatively different units.
source: Waveforms from the putatively same units were more similar than the waveforms from the putatively different units (Figure 3e–g).
evidence: Supported by waveform correlation data shown in Figure 3e-g.

claim: Putatively same units responded similarly to optical stimulation in different sessions.
source: These putatively same units responded similarly to optical stimulation in different sessions (Figure 3h), suggesting a consistent transduction of optical stimulation to LC spiking activity.
evidence: Supported by spike response data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: A consistent transduction of optical stimulation to LC spiking activity exists.
source: These putatively same units responded similarly to optical stimulation in different sessions (Figure 3h), suggesting a consistent transduction of optical stimulation to LC spiking activity.
evidence: Inferred from the similar responses of putatively same units across sessions.

claim: The same pupil exhibited variable dilations to optical stimulation under awake, nontask performing conditions.
source: In contrast to stable LC responses, the same pupil exhibited variable dilations to optical stimulation under awake, nontask performing conditions (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: Supported by pupil response data shown in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: Baseline pupil diameters were similar between sessions and cannot explain the differences in evoked pupil responses.
source: Importantly, baseline pupil diameters were similar (0.71 vs. 0.75 mm, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and thus cannot explain the differences in evoked pupil responses.
evidence: Supported by baseline pupil diameter measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant session-to-session fluctuations of pupil responses were prevalent but not directional.
source: Group data from multiple mice further demonstrated that significant session-to-session fluctuations of pupil responses were prevalent but not directional (solid lines in Figure 4c, d), that is, pupil responses in an earlier session (session 1) were not consistently higher or lower than in a later session (session 2).
evidence: Supported by group data shown in Figure 4c and 4d.

claim: Session-to-session fluctuations were not observable from group comparisons.
source: Therefore, such session-to-session fluctuations were not observable from group comparisons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Privitera et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by group comparison data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citation to Privitera et al., 2020.

claim: Evoked pupil responses fluctuated significantly even with stronger stimulation (50 ms pulses instead of 10 ms) in the awake condition.
source: First, we evoked pupil responses with stronger stimulation (50 ms pulses instead of 10 ms) in the awake condition. While baseline pupil diameters were similar between sessions, evoked pupil responses still fluctuated significantly (Figure 4e, f).
evidence: Supported by pupil response data with 50 ms pulses shown in Figure 4e and 4f.

claim: Pupil exhibited substantial fluctuations in two sessions just several hours apart (4–6 hr).
source: In a subset of experiments, pupil exhibited substantial fluctuations in two sessions just several hours apart (4–6 hr, magenta arrows in Figure 4c–f).
evidence: Supported by data from same-day comparisons indicated by magenta arrows in Figure 4c-f.

claim: Across-session variability of pupil responses was comparable to within-session variability.
source: Further analysis showed that across-session variability of pupil responses was comparable to within-session variability (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Methods).
evidence: Supported by variability analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: For the paired sessions that exhibited significantly different responses to optical stimulation, only a small subset exhibited larger across-session variability than within-session variability.
source: In addition, for the paired sessions that exhibited significantly different responses to optical stimulation (solid lines in Figure 4c–f), only a small subset exhibited larger across-session variability than within-session variability (2 pairs out of 12 under 10 ms condition, and 3 pairs out of 11 under 50 ms condition, Methods).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis described in Methods and data shown in Figure 4c-f.

claim: Evoked pupil responses were noticeably larger under anesthesia compared with the awake condition in the example recordings.
source: Evoked pupil responses were noticeably larger compared with the awake condition in the example recordings, possibly due to a more constricted baseline pupil size under anesthesia (Figure 4g, h, left vs. Figure 4a, b, 0.3 vs. 0.7 mm).
evidence: Supported by comparison of pupil responses between awake and anesthetized conditions shown in Figure 4.

claim: A more constricted baseline pupil size under anesthesia may explain larger evoked pupil responses.
source: Evoked pupil responses were noticeably larger compared with the awake condition in the example recordings, possibly due to a more constricted baseline pupil size under anesthesia (Figure 4g, h, left vs. Figure 4a, b, 0.3 vs. 0.7 mm).
evidence: Speculative explanation based on observed baseline pupil size differences.

claim: Pupil responses to optical stimulation exhibited substantial session-to-session fluctuations under anesthesia.
source: Nevertheless, pupil responses to optical stimulation exhibited substantial session-to-session fluctuations (Figure 4g, h).
evidence: Supported by pupil response data under anesthesia shown in Figure 4g and 4h.

claim: The variations in the relationship between peak pupil diameter and LC cluster size were strongly correlated with hit rate and decision bias during task performance.
source: We found that the variations in the relationship between peak pupil diameter and LC cluster size (as in Figure 1e) were strongly correlated with hit rate and decision bias during task performance (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The correlation between pupil-LC relationship variations and behavioral variables was not likely due to linear fitting of nonlinear relationships.
source: This effect was not likely due to linear fitting of nonlinear relationships (all linear fits are of R2 > 0.85. 0.92 ± 0.05, mean ± SD, n = 9), and the results held when the analysis of pupil–LC relationship was restricted to nonlicking periods only (Figure 5b, Methods).
evidence: Supported by high R2 values of linear fits and analysis restricted to nonlicking periods shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Licking alone cannot fully explain the tight correlation between the variations of the behavioral variables and the variations in the pupil–LC relationship.
source: Therefore, although mice licked more during sessions of higher hit rate and lower decision bias, the results cannot be fully explained by a potentially stronger pupil–LC coupling during licking periods.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of correlations when licking periods were excluded from analysis.

claim: Decision bias-related behavioral variables could explain, at least in part, the variations in the pupil–LC relationship.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that decision bias-related behavioral variables could explain, at least in part, the variations in the pupil–LC relationship.
evidence: Inferred from the strong correlations between behavioral variables and pupil-LC relationship variations.

claim: Fluctuations of behavioral variables reflect state changes such as impulsivity, motivation, and task engagement.
source: Since fluctuations of these behavioral variables reflect state changes such as impulsivity, motivation, and task engagement (Dickinson and Balleine, 1994; Mayrhofer et al., 2013; Berditchevskaia et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2019; McBurney-Lin et al., 2020), our results suggest that the coupling between pupil and LC is state dependent.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work establishing the relationship between behavioral variables and brain states.

claim: The coupling between pupil and LC is state dependent.
source: Since fluctuations of these behavioral variables reflect state changes such as impulsivity, motivation, and task engagement (Dickinson and Balleine, 1994; Mayrhofer et al., 2013; Berditchevskaia et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2019; McBurney-Lin et al., 2020), our results suggest that the coupling between pupil and LC is state dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between behavioral state variables and pupil-LC coupling variations.

claim: Pupil diameter has an overall positive and monotonic relationship with LC spiking activity.
source: In the current study, we have shown that pupil diameter has an overall positive and monotonic relationship with LC spiking activity.
evidence: Supported by data from Figures 1 and 2 showing graded relationships.

claim: Substantial variability exists in the pupil-LC relationship such that only the infrequent and large pupil dilation events (>1.5–2 SD amplitude, <10% occurrence) can accurately predict LC spiking on a moment-by-moment basis.
source: However, substantial variability exists in this relationship that only the infrequent and large pupil dilation events (>1.5–2 SD amplitude, <10% occurrence) can accurately predict LC spiking on a moment-by-moment basis.
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis data from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Pupil responses exhibit large session-to-session fluctuations to identical optical stimulation in the LC.
source: In addition, pupil responses exhibit large session-to-session fluctuations to identical optical stimulation in the LC.
evidence: Supported by data from Figure 4 showing variable pupil responses across sessions.

claim: Averaging multiple repeats/trials of similar pupil responses would yield a much more accurate prediction of LC activity.
source: Together, our results strongly caution treating pupil dilation as a real-time readout of LC activity. Averaging multiple repeats/trials of similar pupil responses would yield a much more accurate prediction of LC activity.
evidence: Inferred from the variability in single-trial pupil-LC relationships.

claim: Large pupil or LC responses have been reported to correlate with a variety of task-related processes, including sensory cue, decision formation, positive feedback, choice bias, and action.
source: Large pupil or LC responses have been reported to correlate with a variety of task-related processes, including sensory cue, decision formation, positive feedback, choice bias, and action (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Usher et al., 1999; Kalwani et al., 2014; Bouret and Richmond, 2015; de Gee et al., 2017; de Gee et al., 2020; Schriver et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The infrequent but strong pupil dilation events can be used as an accurate inference of LC activation in response to sensory stimuli and decision-making processes.
source: In light of this, our work suggests that the infrequent but strong pupil dilation events can be used as an accurate inference of LC activation in response to sensory stimuli and decision-making processes.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of current findings and previous literature on task-related LC/pupil responses.

claim: Pupil and LC likely respond to task-related processes differently, leading to variations in their relationship.
source: However, as discussed below, in general pupil and LC likely respond to task-related processes differently, leading to variations in their relationship.
evidence: Inferred from the observed variability in pupil-LC coupling and session-to-session fluctuations.

claim: Recent evidence has uncovered considerable heterogeneity within the LC nucleus, including molecular compositions, physiological properties, released transmitters, and projection targets.
source: Recent evidence has uncovered considerable heterogeneity within the LC nucleus, including molecular compositions, physiological properties, released transmitters, and projection targets (Robertson et al., 2013; Chandler et al., 2014; Chandler et al., 2019; Schwarz and Luo, 2015; Schwarz et al., 2015; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Uematsu et al., 2017; Totah et al., 2018; Borodovitsyna et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The data support findings of LC heterogeneity.
source: Our data support these findings (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: It is possible that pupil diameter is dynamically coupled with different LC subgroups that are differentially engaged during cognitive processes.
source: Therefore, it is possible that pupil diameter is dynamically coupled with different LC subgroups that are differentially engaged during cognitive processes.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on LC heterogeneity findings.

claim: LC heterogeneity is insufficient to explain the session-to-session fluctuations of pupil responses to LC stimulation.
source: However, this is insufficient to explain the session-to-session fluctuations of pupil responses to LC stimulation, since we likely activated a heterogenous group of LC neurons that exhibited similar session-to-session responses to optical stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from the stable LC responses across sessions despite variable pupil responses.

claim: Slow changes in the tissue due to tetrode/optical fiber implant could alter light transmission to the neurons that were not recorded.
source: The fact that the putatively same neurons tracked across days exhibited similar responses to optical stimulation cannot fully establish the long-term stability of population LC response because slow changes in the tissue due to tetrode/optical fiber implant (gliosis, inflammation, etc.) could alter light transmission to the neurons that were not recorded.
evidence: Speculative consideration of potential confounds based on known biological processes.

claim: Several lines of evidence did not favor the possibility that tissue changes altered light transmission.
source: However, several lines of evidence in our study did not favor this possibility: (1) Pupil responses in a later session did not systematically or progressively differ from an earlier session (e.g., consistently larger or smaller, Figure 4—figure supplement 2); (2) Significant pupil response variability can be observed in sessions that were a few hours apart (Figure 4); (3) Across-session variability of pupil responses was largely comparable to within-session variability (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of data from Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation tends to synchronize neuronal activity, which may not reflect the physiological condition.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation tends to synchronize neuronal activity, which may not reflect the physiological condition (Totah et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and general knowledge about optogenetics.

claim: During wakefulness, the state of the brain is constantly fluctuating, both in the presence and absence of external stimuli.
source: During wakefulness, the state of the brain is constantly fluctuating, both in the presence and absence of external stimuli (Kenet et al., 2003; Fox et al., 2006; Fox and Raichle, 2007; Sakata and Harris, 2009; Luczak et al., 2009; Berkes et al., 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Mohajerani et al., 2013; Romano et al., 2015; Petersen, 2019; McCormick et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work establishing brain state fluctuations.

claim: Pupil response profiles can reflect different behavioral processes.
source: Pupil response profiles can reflect different behavioral processes (Schriver et al., 2020), and pupil responses also can be dissociated from cognitive processes (Podvalny et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pupil responses can be dissociated from cognitive processes.
source: Pupil response profiles can reflect different behavioral processes (Schriver et al., 2020), and pupil responses also can be dissociated from cognitive processes (Podvalny et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The data extend observations that LC and pupil respond to behavioral and cognitive variables differently.
source: Our data extend these observations, supporting that LC and pupil respond to behavioral and cognitive variables differently (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from current findings and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mice licked more during high motivation or high engagement trials.
source: Although mice licked more during high motivation or high engagement trials (Berditchevskaia et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2019; McBurney-Lin et al., 2020), our data show that licking alone cannot account for the tight correlation between the variations of the behavioral variables and the variations in the pupil–LC relationship (Figure 5), suggesting that pupil–LC coupling is brain state dependent.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data from Figure 5.

claim: Pupil size changes have been linked to activity in other brain areas and neuromodulatory systems, including the medial prefrontal cortex, the inferior colliculus, and cholinergic signaling.
source: Pupil size changes have been linked to activity in other brain areas and neuromodulatory systems, including the medial prefrontal cortex, the inferior colliculus, and cholinergic signaling (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; Okun et al., 2019; Kucyi and Parvizi, 2020; Pais-Roldán et al., 2020; Sobczak et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Pupil responses to dorsal raphe stimulation exhibited task uncertainty-dependent variations.
source: A recent study found that pupil responses to dorsal raphe stimulation exhibited task uncertainty-dependent variations (Cazettes et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In high motivation/engagement states, multiple circuits including the LC may synergistically influence pupil size changes, resulting in the apparently stronger pupil–LC coupling.
source: Therefore, it is possible that in high motivation/engagement states, multiple circuits including the LC synergistically influence pupil size changes, resulting in the apparently stronger pupil–LC coupling.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on known circuit interactions and current findings.

claim: Higher engagement states may be intimately associated with more 'uninstructed' movements.
source: Another possibility is that higher engagement states may be intimately associated with more 'uninstructed' movements as revealed by recent work (Musall et al., 2019), which can drive robust neuronal activity throughout the brain (Musall et al., 2019; Steinmetz et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019; Salkoff et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: More frequent movements, both task-related and task-unrelated, during periods of high motivation/engagement may underlie the stronger pupil–LC coupling.
source: Future studies with comprehensive movement monitoring will determine whether more frequent movements, both task-related and task-unrelated, during periods of high motivation/engagement underlie the stronger pupil–LC coupling.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: Changes in pupil diameter under constant luminance are tightly linked to states of arousal and attention.
source: Changes in pupil diameter under constant luminance are tightly linked to states of arousal and attention (McGinley et al., 2015a; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dynamic pupil responses are associated with membrane potential fluctuations, sensory evoked responses, salience detection, error estimation, decision-making, and task performance.
source: Dynamic pupil responses are associated with membrane potential fluctuations, sensory evoked responses, salience detection, error estimation, decision-making, and task performance (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Bijleveld et al., 2009; Nassar et al., 2012; de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2020; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015; McGinley et al., 2015b; Lee and Margolis, 2016; Schriver et al., 2018; Schriver et al., 2020; Kucewicz et al., 2018; Ebitz and Moore, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Pupil diameter has been widely used to monitor brain states and their neural substrates.
source: As a result, pupil diameter has been widely used to monitor brain states and their neural substrates.
evidence: Based on established scientific practice and previous literature.

claim: The locus coeruleus (LC)–noradrenergic system has long been thought to play a critical role in controlling arousal and attention.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC)–noradrenergic system has long been thought to play a critical role in controlling arousal and attention (Aston-Jones et al., 1999; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012), and LC activity closely tracks brain states and cognitive processes (Foote et al., 1980; Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Berridge and Foote, 1991; Aston-Jones et al., 1994; Rajkowski et al., 1994; Usher et al., 1999; Takahashi et al., 2010; Carter et al., 2010; Eschenko et al., 2012; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014; Kalwani et al., 2014; Varazzani et al., 2015; Bouret and Richmond, 2015; Fazlali et al., 2016; Swift et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work establishing the role of LC.

claim: LC activity closely tracks brain states and cognitive processes.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC)–noradrenergic system has long been thought to play a critical role in controlling arousal and attention (Aston-Jones et al., 1999; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012), and LC activity closely tracks brain states and cognitive processes (Foote et al., 1980; Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Berridge and Foote, 1991; Aston-Jones et al., 1994; Rajkowski et al., 1994; Usher et al., 1999; Takahashi et al., 2010; Carter et al., 2010; Eschenko et al., 2012; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014; Kalwani et al., 2014; Varazzani et al., 2015; Bouret and Richmond, 2015; Fazlali et al., 2016; Swift et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Work mainly in the past decade has provided correlative and causal evidence linking pupil size changes to LC activity.
source: Importantly, work mainly in the past decade has provided correlative and causal evidence linking pupil size changes to LC activity (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Murphy et al., 2014; Varazzani et al., 2015; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; de Gee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Hayat et al., 2020; Privitera et al., 2020), leading to the increased utilization of pupil diameter as a noninvasive readout of LC (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Gilzenrat et al., 2010; Preuschoff et al., 2011; Konishi et al., 2017; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2019; Aminihajibashi et al., 2020; Clewett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Pupil diameter has been increasingly utilized as a noninvasive readout of LC.
source: Importantly, work mainly in the past decade has provided correlative and causal evidence linking pupil size changes to LC activity (Rajkowski et al., 1994; Murphy et al., 2014; Varazzani et al., 2015; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; de Gee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Hayat et al., 2020; Privitera et al., 2020), leading to the increased utilization of pupil diameter as a noninvasive readout of LC (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Gilzenrat et al., 2010; Preuschoff et al., 2011; Konishi et al., 2017; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2019; Aminihajibashi et al., 2020; Clewett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work and inferred from the trend in the field.

claim: A few recent studies demonstrated that the correlation between pupil and LC could be neuron- and task epoch-specific.
source: However, a few recent studies demonstrated that the correlation between pupil and LC could be neuron- and task epoch-specific (Joshi et al., 2016; Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Yang et al., 2021), raising the possibility that pupil diameter can be dissociated from LC activity.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pupil diameter can be dissociated from LC activity.
source: However, a few recent studies demonstrated that the correlation between pupil and LC could be neuron- and task epoch-specific (Joshi et al., 2016; Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Yang et al., 2021), raising the possibility that pupil diameter can be dissociated from LC activity.
evidence: Inferred from neuron- and task epoch-specific correlations reported in previous studies.

claim: 19 single unit recordings from 7 mice performing the single-whisker detection task were extracted.
source: For Figures 1 and 2, 19 single unit recordings (cluster quality measure Lratio: 0.01 ± 0.005; firing rate: 1.65 ± 0.25 spikes/s; percent ISI <10 ms: 0.11% ± 0.1%) from 7 mice performing the single-whisker detection task (see below) were extracted using MClust (Redish, 2014), among which six recordings were from our previous dataset (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Explicit description of experimental data collection.

claim: Six recordings were from a previous dataset.
source: For Figures 1 and 2, 19 single unit recordings (cluster quality measure Lratio: 0.01 ± 0.005; firing rate: 1.65 ± 0.25 spikes/s; percent ISI <10 ms: 0.11% ± 0.1%) from 7 mice performing the single-whisker detection task (see below) were extracted using MClust (Redish, 2014), among which six recordings were from our previous dataset (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Explicit statement with citation to previous work.

claim: 5 units from 5 mice were tracked over time (between 1 and 5 days).
source: For Figure 3, 5 units from 5 mice were tracked over time (between 1 and 5 days).
evidence: Explicit description of experimental data collection.

claim: 68 pupil sessions (34 baseline pupil-matched session pairs) to LC stimulation were acquired from 8 mice.
source: For Figure 4, 68 pupil sessions (34 baseline pupil-matched session pairs) to LC stimulation were acquired from 8 mice, 4 of which were implanted with an optical fiber only (0.39 NA, 200 µm core), and the time between sessions 1 and 2 was 4.4 ± 0.9 days.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental data collection.

claim: The time between sessions 1 and 2 was 4.4 ± 0.9 days.
source: For Figure 4, 68 pupil sessions (34 baseline pupil-matched session pairs) to LC stimulation were acquired from 8 mice, 4 of which were implanted with an optical fiber only (0.39 NA, 200 µm core), and the time between sessions 1 and 2 was 4.4 ± 0.9 days.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental parameters.

claim: Mice were trained to perform a head-fixed, Go/NoGo single-whisker detection task.
source: In brief, mice were trained to perform a head-fixed, Go/NoGo single-whisker detection task, in which mice reported whether they perceived a brief deflection (0.5 s, 40 Hz or 0.2 s, 25 Hz sinusoidal deflection) to the right C2 whisker by licking toward a water port.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental methods.

claim: Mice reported whether they perceived a brief deflection to the right C2 whisker by licking toward a water port.
source: In brief, mice were trained to perform a head-fixed, Go/NoGo single-whisker detection task, in which mice reported whether they perceived a brief deflection (0.5 s, 40 Hz or 0.2 s, 25 Hz sinusoidal deflection) to the right C2 whisker by licking toward a water port.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental methods.

claim: A 0.1-s auditory cue (8 kHz tone, ~80 dB SPL) was introduced starting 1–1.5 s before stimulus onset.
source: A 0.1-s auditory cue (8 kHz tone, ~80 dB SPL) was introduced starting 1–1.5 s before stimulus onset.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental methods.

claim: Ambient white noise (~80 dB SPL) was played to mask any other potential auditory cues associated with movement of the piezo stimulator.
source: During all sessions, ambient white noise (cutoff at 40 kHz, ~80 dB SPL) was played through a separate speaker to mask any other potential auditory cues associated with movement of the piezo stimulator.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental methods.

claim: Video of the left pupil was acquired at 50 Hz or 20 Hz.
source: Video of the left pupil (ipsilateral to LC recording and stimulation) was acquired at 50 Hz using a PhotonFocus camera and StreamPix 5 software, or at 20 Hz using a Basler acA1300-200 µm camera and Pylon software.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental methods.

claim: The left pupil was ipsilateral to LC recording and stimulation.
source: Video of the left pupil (ipsilateral to LC recording and stimulation) was acquired at 50 Hz using a PhotonFocus camera and StreamPix 5 software, or at 20 Hz using a Basler acA1300-200 µm camera and Pylon software.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental setup.

claim: An ambient blue LED was used to constrict the pupil and to mask any potential light leak.
source: An ambient blue LED was used to constrict the pupil and to mask any potential light leak.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental methods.

claim: <15 mW (RMS) of blue light was measured at the tip of optical fiber.
source: <15 mW (RMS) of blue light was measured at the tip of optical fiber.
evidence: Explicit description of experimental parameters.

claim: Stimulation patterns were delivered every 10–30 s and randomized.
source: Stimulation patterns were delivered every 10–30 s and randomized.

claim: If the interval between two adjacent spikes was shorter than median inter-spike interval of that unit, the spikes were grouped into a single cluster.
